stories.headline: Teenage boy killed, four injured by lightning strike on Mount Blue Sky
stories.summary:
A 15-year-old boy was killed and four others were injured when lightning struck a hiking party on the summit of Mount Blue Sky on Sunday afternoon, according to the Clear Creek County Sheriff's Office. The deceased victim was identified as Levi Strobel of an undisclosed hometown. Emergency personnel arrived on scene and attempted to revive Strobel but were unsuccessful.

Strobel's younger brother, who was also in the five-person hiking party, was airlifted to a Denver hospital. Two adult men in the group sustained minor injuries and were not hospitalized. A fifth person unconnected to the group also sustained minor injuries and was not transported.

Strobel's family issued a statement saying the teenager had sought to protect his younger brother before being struck. The family described Strobel as someone who brought "immeasurable joy" to those around him. The Clear Creek County Coroner's Office released the family's statement Monday.

Mount Blue Sky, formerly known as Mount Evans, is a popular fourteener in Clear Creek County accessible by road. Afternoon lightning storms are a common and serious hazard on Colorado's high peaks during summer months.

stories.headline: Passenger shot and killed in Littleton after Jefferson County hit-and-run, suspect not yet arrested
stories.summary:
A 23-year-old man died Saturday night after being shot in the head in an incident Jefferson County investigators believe stemmed from a hit-and-run in Littleton. The driver of a blue Ford F-150 pulled into the Columbine High School parking lot shortly after 10:30 p.m. Saturday, where paramedics transported his passenger, Andrew Bott, to the hospital; Bott later died from his injuries.

Investigators believe the shooting is connected to an earlier hit-and-run near South Santa Fe Drive and West Belleview Avenue, where the same blue Ford F-150 reportedly struck several vehicles and fled. The shooting occurred approximately three miles from the initial hit-and-run, near Grant Ranch Boulevard and West Bowles Avenue. One of the hit-and-run victims called police to report following the Ford, and police advised him to stop pursuit while issuing a be-on-the-lookout alert.

As of Monday afternoon, no arrest had been made. Investigators executed a search warrant at a Highlands Ranch home Sunday night and interviewed two people, but no additional details were released about those individuals.

The Jefferson County Sheriff's Office is asking drivers with dash camera footage and businesses or residents along West Bowles Avenue between South Santa Fe Drive and Grant Ranch Boulevard to review surveillance video from between 10:25 p.m. and 10:35 p.m. Saturday. Tips can be submitted to 303-271-5612 or jcsocrimetips@jeffco.us.

stories.headline: Colorado approves $3.9 million in incentives to keep Alterra Mountain Co. headquarters in Denver
stories.summary:
The Colorado Economic Development Commission approved a package of incentives Monday totaling $3.9 million to help Alterra Mountain Co. relocate its corporate headquarters from the RiNo neighborhood to Upper Downtown Denver. The package includes a $1 million no-interest loan, a $1 million grant, and $1.9 million in Job Growth Incentive Tax Credits tied to the creation of 106 additional jobs paying an average annual salary of $131,071.

Alterra, the creator of the Ikon Pass and owner of 19 North American ski resorts including Steamboat Springs and Arapahoe Basin, had indicated it was also considering relocating to Salt Lake City. The urgency of the approval — the EDC held an unusual 7 a.m. Monday meeting — signals state officials viewed the threat as credible. Alterra had already secured a $7 million loan from the Downtown Denver Development Authority, approved in an unusually rapid process.

The new headquarters building is expected to serve as an anchor for a broader outdoor recreation business hub in Upper Downtown, where large office towers have been selling at discounts of 90% or more from pre-pandemic prices. The $1 million grant includes provisions for smaller awards of up to $250,000 to outdoor recreation companies that co-locate with Alterra in the building.

Alterra also manages Winter Park Resort under a 50-year lease with the City and County of Denver. The state incentives are conditioned on Alterra completing the move and meeting job creation benchmarks.

stories.headline: Denver Health faces $65 million in annual Medicaid cuts by 2032 as federal policy changes loom
stories.summary:
Denver Health, the city's primary safety-net hospital, faces $65 million in annual Medicaid funding cuts by 2032 as a result of federal policy changes, according to a report from the Denver Business Journal. The cuts threaten the 166-year-old institution's core mission of serving uninsured and low-income patients across the Denver metro area.

Denver Health serves a disproportionately high share of Medicaid and uninsured patients compared to other regional hospitals, making it especially vulnerable to federal reimbursement reductions. Hospital officials have warned that the funding shortfall could force difficult decisions about services, staffing, and the network of community clinics the hospital operates.

The looming cuts come as Denver Health is already managing financial pressures stemming from post-pandemic patient volume shifts and rising operational costs. The hospital system operates more than a dozen community health centers across Denver in addition to its main campus.

City and state officials have historically relied on Denver Health to provide services that other hospitals do not, including trauma care, behavioral health services, and care for the homeless population. The potential funding reduction has renewed calls for state-level action to offset the impact.

stories.headline: Denver Public Schools superintendent Alex Marrero to remain in post after four-hour board meeting
stories.summary:
The Denver Public Schools Board of Education announced no changes to Superintendent Alex Marrero's employment following a nearly four-hour meeting Monday, during which the board spent most of its time in closed session with an outside attorney and separately with Marrero. Board President Xóchitl Gaytán confirmed afterward that "nothing has changed" with the superintendency.

The meeting was called after Marrero sent a letter to Gaytán in June alleging that board members were overstepping their authority under the district's policy governance model, which reserves day-to-day operational decisions for the superintendent rather than the board. Marrero's letter raised questions about whether he was signaling intent to resign, as his contract allows him to exit with 30 days' notice if the board abandons policy governance.

Board members have expressed concern about Marrero's commitment to DPS after he was a finalist for superintendent positions in Miami and Chicago last year, failing to secure either role. Some directors have also called the district's implementation of policy governance "extreme" and argued the board should play a more active role in areas such as student literacy.

The board agreed to work through governance concerns at a retreat next month. Director Marlene De La Rosa said she was "fully committed" to building a better relationship between the board and the superintendent, but the underlying tensions over the governance model and Marrero's future with the district remain unresolved.

stories.headline: Denver DSA mobilizes to hold at-large City Council seat in November special election
stories.summary:
The Denver chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America is preparing to compete in a special election this November for the at-large Denver City Council seat being vacated by Councilwoman Sarah Parady, who announced in June she would resign in August due to health problems. The group is energized by last month's primary victory of DSA-backed candidate Melat Kiros over longtime U.S. Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado's 1st Congressional District.

The November special election will be decided by a simple plurality, meaning a candidate can win with less than a majority of votes. That differs from the April 2027 election for the same seat, which will require more than 50% or trigger a runoff. The unusual structure is expected to attract a large field of candidates and could advantage an organized, motivated political faction like the DSA.

Parady is expected to formally resign on Aug. 5, after which candidates will have a short window to file for the special election. Seven people have already filed for the same seat's regular April election. The DSA will conduct an internal endorsement process before committing to a candidate.

The contest will serve as a significant test of whether the DSA's recent momentum in Denver's congressional race translates to municipal politics. The at-large seat is one of two on the 13-member council elected citywide, giving it broad visibility across Denver neighborhoods.

stories.headline: Aspen Acres Fire reaches 101,921 acres; all evacuation orders lifted as containment holds at 66%
stories.summary:
The Aspen Acres Fire burning in Custer and Pueblo counties has grown to 101,921 acres and is now 66% contained, according to a Monday morning update from the incident management team. All evacuation orders have been lifted, with all zones now in either pre-evacuation or clear status; residents in pre-evacuation zones still require a re-entry card to return home.

The fire, which started June 29 approximately 10 miles northwest of Rye, has destroyed more than 850 structures including at least 350 homes, making it one of Colorado's most destructive wildfires by structures lost. It has become the seventh-largest fire in Colorado state history by acreage. No casualties have been reported.

More than 880 personnel are working to achieve full containment. Crews are focused on strengthening fire lines along the west side of the blaze, and tactical burning of the fire's interior is continuing when conditions allow. Fire managers warned that warmer conditions in the coming days may increase fire behavior slightly, though overall activity is expected to remain minimal.

Flooding risk at the burn scar remains elevated. More than 85 volunteers helped fill and load sandbags on Sunday to protect communities from potential post-fire flooding. The cause of the fire has been determined to be human-caused, though the exact origin and manner remain under investigation.

stories.headline: Colorado bankruptcy filings jump 23% in June, with increases in Boulder, Broomfield and Weld counties
stories.summary:
Colorado bankruptcy filings rose 23% in June compared with the same month a year earlier, according to data reported by BizWest. The increase was driven largely by higher filing rates in Boulder, Broomfield, and Weld counties, while Larimer County saw a decrease.

The spike in filings tracks a broader national trend of rising personal and business bankruptcies as elevated interest rates and persistent inflation continue to strain household and corporate finances. Colorado's increase outpaced the national average for the month.

The data does not break down the filings by type, but rising Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 personal bankruptcies have been observed across Colorado's Front Range communities in recent months. Business bankruptcies have also ticked upward in several metro Denver sectors.

The trend adds to concerns about the financial health of Colorado consumers and small businesses amid an uncertain economic environment, and comes as the state's unemployment rate has held relatively steady at 3.9%.

stories.headline: Downtown Denver Development Authority to spend $300,000 on major Olive Moya mural at Denver Pavilions
stories.summary:
The Downtown Denver Development Authority is commissioning a $300,000 mural by Denver artist Olive Moya to cover the southwest-facing exterior walls of the Denver Pavilions complex along 15th Street, between Welton Street and Tremont Place. Work began this week, and the project is expected to be completed in early August. The mural will span approximately 46,500 square feet across two walls reaching as high as 97 feet.

The commission replaces a vinyl banner featuring an image of artist Clyfford Still that had hung on one of the walls for several years. Funding comes from Denver Pavilions operating revenues including parking and commercial leases, following the DDDA's $37 million purchase of the 350,000-square-foot complex last year and an additional $8 million earmarked for capital improvements.

Moya said she designed the mural to "reflect the inevitability of change and the ongoing evolution of a city." Denver Arts & Venues curator Michael Chavez called the work a "vibrant visual landmark" that celebrates Denver's creative community. The installation is being handled by Art in Context, a firm specializing in large-scale public art.

The mural is the first visible sign of a broader facelift at Denver Pavilions, which an Urban Land Institute report earlier this year described as suffering a slow decline along the 16th Street pedestrian mall. The DDDA plans to spend approximately $3 million on additional capital improvements including the parking garage, roof, and signage.

stories.headline: DSA national co-chair defends calls to abolish Senate, ICE, and borders in Fox News interview
stories.summary:
Democratic Socialists of America co-chair Megan Romer reaffirmed the organization's positions on abolishing the U.S. Senate, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and national borders in a Fox News Sunday interview, drawing national attention as the DSA's political influence grows following a string of primary victories this summer. Romer also expressed support for defunding the Pentagon, replacing the Supreme Court and presidency "as we know them," and public ownership of most large corporations.

The interview carries local relevance given the DSA's rising profile in Denver, where DSA-backed Melat Kiros won last month's Democratic primary in Colorado's 1st Congressional District over longtime incumbent Diana DeGette. Kiros is now favored in the general election for the heavily Democratic Denver-based district, and the Denver DSA chapter is separately organizing for a city council special election this fall.

Romer described several of the more radical policy goals as part of a "long-term" agenda, saying open borders are "part of a longer-term, international plan" rather than an immediate objective. She argued that eliminating poverty-driven crime would over time reduce the need for mass incarceration.

Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson and Majority Leader Steve Scalise both highlighted Romer's comments on social media, framing the November midterm elections as a choice between mainstream governance and socialist policy. Centrist Democrats including Van Jones and Bill Maher have also publicly pushed back against the party's leftward shift.

stories.headline: Rockies routed 11-2 by Brewers as Milwaukee pitcher Misiorowski sets strikeout records
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies were beaten 11-2 by the Milwaukee Brewers on Sunday, with Brewers starter Jacob Misiorowski delivering one of the most dominant pitching performances in recent MLB history. Misiorowski struck out 12 of the first 13 batters he faced — including each of the first seven — and allowed only one hit over five innings, setting a Brewers franchise record for consecutive strikeouts to open a game.

Sixty-six of Misiorowski's 83 pitches exceeded 100 mph, breaking his own major league record for most 100-mph pitches in a single game since pitch tracking began in 2008. The Rockies' only hit off Misiorowski came on a two-out home run by Cole Carrigg in the fifth inning on a 101.9-mph fastball — the fastest pitch to result in a Rockies homer in the pitch-tracking era. Misiorowski improved to 11-4 with an MLB-best 1.58 ERA and leads the majors with 185 strikeouts.

Colorado starter Kyle Freeland allowed five runs in 5.1 innings, his ERA rising to 7.34 as he fell to 2-10 on the season. The Brewers had a season-high 11 extra-base hits, including nine doubles that matched a Milwaukee franchise single-game record.

The Rockies are off Monday before beginning a two-game series in San Diego on Tuesday. Michael Lorenzen, 3-9 with a 6.53 ERA, is scheduled to start for Colorado against the Padres' Michael King.

stories.headline: Rapids defender Lucas Herrington reflects on World Cup penalty miss, aims to regain form
stories.summary:
Colorado Rapids defender Lucas Herrington has spoken publicly about missing a penalty kick during the 2026 World Cup, describing the experience as the most difficult of his professional career. Herrington, who has returned to Rapids training, said he is focused on working through the moment mentally and physically as the club's MLS season continues.

Herrington's miss came in a high-stakes World Cup match and drew significant attention given the tournament was hosted in North America, including matches played in the United States. The defender said the support of his Rapids teammates has been important during the transition back to club play.

The Rapids are in the midst of their MLS regular season and are looking to Herrington to return to the form that earned him international selection. Head coach and club officials have expressed confidence in Herrington's ability to contribute going forward.

Herrington's situation reflects the broader emotional toll that high-pressure international tournament moments can have on players who must quickly return to demanding club schedules. His performance in upcoming Rapids matches will be closely watched by both club supporters and national team observers.

topStory.headline: Earthquake Collapses Shopping Mall in Southern Japan, Multiple Deaths Reported in Kumamoto Prefecture
topStory.summary:
A 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck southern Japan's Kumamoto Prefecture on Tuesday afternoon local time, triggering fires, collapsing buildings, and causing an explosion at a major shopping mall that left multiple people dead and many others trapped. The Japan Meteorological Agency recorded the quake at magnitude 7.1, reaching the highest possible intensity level of seven on Japan's Shindo shaking scale, while the U.S. Geological Survey measured it at 6.8. The tremor hit at 4:27 p.m. local time, with aftershocks continuing for at least 30 minutes, including a magnitude 4.2 aftershock reported around 7 p.m.

The most severe incident occurred at the Aeon Mall in Kashima Town, where an explosion of undetermined cause caused the second floor of the building to partially collapse, trapping an unknown number of people inside. Police told Japanese broadcaster TBS there were "quite a few" presumed dead at the site, and a local police source described "a lot of deaths," though authorities had not released an official death toll as of early reports. Emergency crews were conducting search and rescue operations at the mall, while mall operator Aeon said it was evacuating customers and assessing the situation.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi confirmed injuries and widespread infrastructure damage, urging residents to evacuate to safe locations and remain alert. NHK footage showed collapsed and burning buildings, large road cracks, a buckled elevated highway, and a derailed freight train. Approximately 40,000 to 45,000 households lost electricity in the Kumamoto region, and mobile phone services were disrupted in some areas. Chipmaker TSMC evacuated workers from its nearby plant as a precaution.

Authorities initially issued a tsunami warning for southwestern coastlines of Kyushu island but lifted it after a few hours. The Nuclear Regulation Authority reported no abnormalities at nuclear power plants in the region, and Kyushu Electric Power confirmed that three operating reactors were functioning normally. Japan is one of the world's most seismically active nations, experiencing hundreds of earthquakes each year.

The disaster drew immediate comparisons to the 2016 Kumamoto earthquakes, a sequence that included a magnitude 6.5 and a magnitude 7.3 tremor two days apart, killing between 273 and 278 people and injuring more than 2,700. Residents and local officials described Tuesday's shaking as reminiscent of that event. With search and rescue operations ongoing and casualty figures still being confirmed, the full scale of deaths and damage remained uncertain.
